Conclusion: In this preclinical study, AHUP-CPR alone or with REBOA, significantly increased 24-hour survival rate and hemodynamics compared with C-CPR+REBOA.
nd30e8d30e1c3: Background: Oxygen administration following cardiac arrest (CA) is associated with cardiac dysfunction, brain injury, and poor survival. These injuries are driven in part by mitochondrial injury, but the metabolic consequences of post-CA hyperoxia remain incompletely understood. We hypothesized that post-CA hyperoxia produces histotoxic dysoxia — impaired cellular oxygen utilization despite adequate arterial oxygenation. Methods: In a murine model of CA, mice underwent 12 minutes of asystole followed by CPR. Beginning 30 minutes post-resuscitation, mice were exposed to 30% O 2 for 6 hours. Systemic metabolic parameters, including core body temperature, whole-body oxygen consumption (V̇O 2 ), and arterial blood gas values (pH, PO 2 , SaO 2 ) were assessed. Results: Post-CA exposure to 30% O 2 induced a systemic metabolic crisis characterized by hypothermia (35.0±0.3 vs. 37.3±0.1°C, p<0.005, n=3-4) and markedly suppressed V̇O 2 (2.1±1.0 vs. 9.1±1.3 mL/kg/min, p<0.001, n=5) compared to sham animals receiving identical oxygen treatment. Arterial blood gas analysis demonstrated severe acidosis (pH 6.91±0.03 vs. 7.19±0.01, p<0.001, n=8-10). Notably, arterial PO 2 and SaO 2 were preserved and did not differ from sham (p>0.05, n=8-10), indicating that metabolic injury occurred independently of arterial hypoxemia. Conclusions: Post-CA hyperoxia produced systemic hypothermia, suppressed whole-body oxygen consumption, and severe acidosis. Despite normal arterial PO 2 and SaO 2 , these findings indicate a failure of cellular oxygen utilization rather than delivery. This pattern is consistent with histotoxic dysoxia and implicates mitochondrial dysfunction as a central mechanism of post-resuscitation metabolic injury.
n4c03d7993bf4: Objective: Post-cardiac arrest syndrome (PCAS) is characterized by a rapid, dysregulated inflammatory response that exacerbates organ injury and undermines recovery. Extracellular vesicle-encapsulated mitochondrial DNA has recently been identified as a potent stimulus of post-resuscitation immune cell activation via the cyclic GMP-AMP synthase-stimulator of interferon genes (cGAS-STING) pathway. Whether pharmacological cGAS inhibition can attenuate the post-resuscitation inflammatory response in vivo is unknown. Accordingly, we tested the hypothesis that cGAS inhibition attenuates the early post-resuscitation transcriptomic inflammatory response in peripheral blood mononuclear cells (PBMCs) after cardiac arrest. Methods: Swine (n=14) underwent 7 minutes of ventricular fibrillation cardiac arrest and subsequent resuscitation. After return of spontaneous circulation (ROSC), animals were randomized to receive a small molecule inhibitor of cGAS (G140; 0.1 mg/kg IV; n=7) or vehicle (n=7) at 15 minutes post-ROSC. PBMCs were isolated at baseline and 4 hours post-ROSC for bulk RNA sequencing. Differentially expressed genes (DEGs) were identified using DESeq2 (adjusted p<0.05). Results: PBMCs from vehicle-treated animals exhibited 3,145 DEGs at 4 hours post-ROSC compared with baseline, reflecting widespread transcriptomic activation. G140-treated animals exhibited only 719 DEGs (77% reduction vs. vehicle; Figure, A ). Expression of cGAS itself was unchanged, consistent with pharmacological inhibition of enzymatic activity rather than gene expression. However, TBK1, the kinase immediately downstream of STING that phosphorylates IRF3, was significantly downregulated in G140-treated animals (log 2 FC=–0.39, p_adj=0.04). Additional genes within the cGAS-STING and innate immune signaling pathways were suppressed in G140- vs. vehicle-treated animals, including NLRP3, IL-15, TNFRSF11A, CCL14, and CCL21 ( Figure, B ). Conclusion: Systemic cGAS inhibition with G140 administered shortly after ROSC markedly attenuates the early post-resuscitation transcriptomic inflammatory response in porcine PBMCs. These findings support cGAS-STING as a tractable therapeutic target and provide rationale for further evaluation of cGAS inhibition as a targeted immunomodulatory strategy in PCAS.
n5dd5507f32f1: Introduction: The role of pyroptosis, a highly inflammatory form of programmed cell death, in cardiac injury following cardiac arrest is unknown. Related to pyroptosis, our prior work has shown that both oxidant injury and intracellular NAD levels result in significant cardiac injury and protection respectively. A better understanding of how oxidant stress and NAD metabolism affect cardiomyocyte injury and pyroptosis could identify new targets for cardiac arrest care. Hypothesis: We hypothesize that cardiac oxidant exposure induces NAD depletion and pyroptosis, which can be rescued by replenishment of cellular NAD. Methods: H9C2 cardiomyocytes were exposed to H 2 O 2 to create oxidative stress. Cell morphological change was observed under microscope, and cell viability was measured by CCK8 kit based on intracellular LDH activity. The expressions of GSDMD and GSDME and their N-terminal fragments were assessed by Western blot analysis. Intracellular NAD content was measured by assay kit. Results: H 2 O 2 induced a dose-dependent death of H9C2 cardiomyocytes, which plateaued at 1 mM and this death was related to NAD + depletion. H9C2 cells exhibited characteristic morphological changes of pyroptosis, such as cell swelling and rupture of the cell membrane, and release of LDH. Supplement with 1 mM NAM, a NAD + precursor, partially rescued viability in H 2 O 2 -treated cells from 54.9 ±1.7% to 81.7 ± 2.2% at 4h (p<0.01). The Nampt inhibitor FK866 (1 μM), which blocks NAD synthesis, totally nullified the protective effect of NAM on cell viability. The pan-caspase inhibitor Z-vad (100 μM) blocked the typical morphology of pyroptosis induced by H 2 O 2 . NAM also restored NAD + concentrations. To determine which gasdermin is involved in oxidant-induced cell death, cardiomyocytes were treated with 1 mM H 2 O 2 for up to 5 hrs. Both GSDME and its Asp270 cleavage N-terminal fragment were observed, and GSDME-N expression peaked after 2h exposure to H 2 O 2 . It was blocked by treatment with NAM or a caspase 3 inhibitor, but not by the NLRP3 inhibitor MCC950. Although GSDMD was cleaved after 2h exposure, there was no expression of the cleaved GSDMD (Asp275) N-terminal fragment. Conclusion: Cardiac oxidant injury, known to occur during cardiac arrest, can result in pyroptotic cell death that is mediated by caspases and can be rescued by NAD precursor treatment.
n718c839d5a68: Introduction: In austere settings, prolonged bag-valve-mask (BVM) ventilation may be required before advanced airway support is available. Excessive inspiratory flow, elevated airway pressures, and inconsistent tidal volumes during sustained manual ventilation increase the risk of lung injury and provider fatigue. Sotair is a flow-modulating accessory designed to improve ventilation safety during prolonged manual ventilation. Hypothesis: We hypothesized that Sotair would improve ventilation safety by limiting excessive inspiratory flow, airway pressure, and tidal volume delivery while maintaining physiologic stability compared to ventilation with a sham device. Methods: Twenty-two juvenile domestic swine (mean weight 52 ± 4 kg) were enrolled and assigned to 6-hour (n=8) or 24-hour (n=14) ventilation cohorts in a non-survival model of prolonged manual overventilation. Animals underwent intubation, invasive hemodynamic monitoring, hourly arterial blood gas sampling, and prolonged manual ventilation with a BVM system using either an active Sotair or sham device. Respiratory rate was titrated to end-tidal CO 2, and sham ventilation was delivered with forceful manual respirations to model excessive ventilation conditions. Airway flow, peak airway pressure, and tidal volume were continuously recorded, and gross lung injury was assessed at necropsy. Longitudinal physiologic data were analyzed using generalized estimating equations and mixed-effects regression models. Results: Twenty-one animals were analyzed after protocol violation: 8 in the 6-hour cohort (4 sham, 4 Sotair) and 13 in the 24-hour cohort (7 sham, 6 Sotair). Across 124,350 breaths over 360 observation hours, Sotair significantly reduced average inspiratory flow (–46.63 L/min), peak airway pressure (–33.04 cmH 2 O), and tidal volume (–312.52 mL) compared with sham ventilation (all p<0.001). In the 24-hour cohort, Sotair was associated with improved oxygenation stability, including higher ABG-derived arterial oxygen saturation at 24 hours compared with sham (+3.34%, p=0.031), lower continuous pulse oximetry-derived oxygen saturation coefficient of variation (1.73% vs 4.26%, p<0.0001), and lower partial pressure carbon dioxide coefficient of variation (12.01% vs 15.29%, p<0.0001). Gross lung injury scores did not differ significantly between treatment groups overall, although injury severity was greater in 24-hour than in 6-hour animals independent of device assignment (p=0.003). Conclusions: Flow modulation using Sotair reduced excessive inspiratory flow, airway pressure, and tidal volume during prolonged manual ventilation while maintaining physiologic stability. Although gross injury outcomes were not significantly different between groups, these findings support further evaluation of Sotair as a low-resource adjunct for prolonged field care and austere settings.
ne71b5cbfd84a: Background: During prehospital airway and ventilatory emergencies including respiratory emergencies, airway compromise, and out-of-hospital cardiac arrest (OHCA), ventilation delivered by prehospital providers often exceeds recommended airway pressures and ventilation rates. Elevated inspiratory pressures increase intrathoracic pressure, impair venous return, and promote gastric insufflation, increasing the risk of regurgitation and aspiration. Supraglottic airway devices (SGAs) are widely used in emergency medical services because they can be placed rapidly and have high first-pass success rates. However, limited physiologic data describe how SGA design affects esophageal pressure transmission under high-pressure ventilation conditions typical of prehospital resuscitation. Hypothesis: Second-generation SGAs with dual gastric channels will reduce gastric insufflation and distention, reflected by lower esophageal pressures, compared with single-channel devices under conditions simulating cardiac arrest ventilation. Goal: This study compared esophageal pressure transmission and gastric venting among SGAs during pressure-controlled ventilation simulating prehospital cardiac arrest. Methods: In a controlled cadaveric study, fresh unfixed human cadavers were ventilated with multiple SGAs; an endotracheal tube served as the reference standard. Pressure-controlled ventilation was delivered at inspiratory pressures of 20, 30, 40, and 50 cmH 2 O to replicate prehospital ventilation extremes. Distal esophageal pressure was measured continuously through a cannula inserted through the abdominal wall into the stomach and secured in the distal esophagus. Airway placement was confirmed bronchoscopically, and airflow through gastric channels and oropharyngeal leak pathways was assessed. Results: As inspiratory pressure increased, esophageal pressure rose across all devices. Dual-channel second-generation SGAs transmitted lower esophageal pressures than single-channel and first-generation devices, indicating reduced gastric insufflation and distention under high-pressure ventilation. Conclusion: SGA design significantly influences esophageal pressure transmission during cardiac arrest ventilation. Dual-channel second-generation SGAs reduce esophageal pressurization, suggesting a mechanism to mitigate gastric distention during CPR. These findings have direct implications for OHCA airway strategy, supporting device selection and ventilation approaches that minimize hyperventilation and its downstream hemodynamic consequences during resuscitation.
nc5bcbaf4c74d: Introduction: During CPR, chest compressions induce oscillations in the capnogram that can be quantified as the Capnogram Oscillation Magnitude (COM) and the Airway Opening Index (AOI). These metrics are hypothesized to reflect airway patency and effective ventilation. Positive end-expiratory pressure (PEEP) may modulate capnographic waveform morphology during CPR, though the relationship between PEEP, COM, AOI, and hemodynamics remains poorly understood. Aim: We examined the effect of titrated PEEP on capnographic waveform morphology, including COM, AOI, and peak end-tidal carbon dioxide (ETCO2) during mechanical CPR in a pilot study using a swine model of ventricular fibrillation (VF) cardiac arrest. Methods: Four swine underwent 8 minutes of untreated VF followed by 60 minutes of mechanical CPR. Animals were intubated and ventilated at 10 breaths/min with fraction of inspired oxygen of 1.0. PEEP was sequentially titrated across 6-minute epochs of 0, 5, and 10 cmH 2 O in repeated cycles during CPR. 6 doses of epinephrine (0.02 mg/kg) were administered beginning at minute 14 and repeated every 4 minutes. Continuous capnography and aortic blood pressure were recorded throughout. A custom MATLAB algorithm was used to calculate COM and AOI. Results: Across 4 animals, we observed that stepwise increases in PEEP from 0 to 5 to 10 cmH2O were associated with longer time to peak ETCO2 within ventilation cycles (Figure 1). We observed no overall changes in aortic pressure or ETCO2 with PEEP titrations, but these did gradually decrease over the course of resuscitation (Figure 2). Conclusion: In this preliminary swine model of cardiac arrest, increasing PEEP appeared to influence capnographic waveform morphology during mechanical CPR, particularly the time to peak ETCO2 after a ventilation. Aortic blood pressure and overall ETCO2 remained largely stable during stepwise PEEP titration, but decreased over the course of resuscitation. This association may indicate that at higher PEEP levels cardiac output exceeds ventilation, resulting in the prolonged time to peak ETCO2. Ongoing analysis will quantify the dose-dependent effects of PEEP on ventilation metrics (AOI, COM, and peak ETCO2), along with indicators of cardiac output (aortic blood pressure and the area under the capnography waveform curve). These findings may inform PEEP as a modifiable ventilation parameter during CPR to optimize airway management and resuscitation outcomes.
nf9222264f10d: Background: Psychiatric morbidity is common after out-of-hospital cardiac arrest (OHCA), yet whether survivors carry excess risk relative to other critically ill patients or instead share post-intensive care syndrome (PICS) mechanisms remains unclear. Hypothesis: OHCA survivors experience excess new-onset mental health and addictions (MHA) risk compared with matched critical illness survivors, beyond what is explained by pre-existing psychiatric history and sociodemographic vulnerability. Methods: Population-based retrospective cohort study (ICES, Ontario, Canada; 2007-2022). Adults surviving ICU admission for non-traumatic OHCA were matched to non-OHCA critical illness survivors by age (±3 years) and admission date (±3 days). Primary outcome: time to first new-onset MHA diagnosis within 15 years of discharge, from validated physician-coded inpatient, emergency department (ED), and outpatient records. We fit flexible parametric (Royston-Parmar) survival models with death as a competing risk and used logistic regression to compare inpatient versus outpatient care intensity, adjusting for sex, comorbidities, prior healthcare use, and neighbourhood marginalization. Results: Among 6,034 OHCA survivors matched to 16,461 controls (mean follow-up 4.7 years), 2,740 OHCA survivors (45.4%) received a new MHA diagnosis: anxiety/mood (33.9%), substance-related (7.8%), and psychotic disorders (2.7%); 20.0% required inpatient psychiatric admission. Incidence peaked within six months post-discharge. Composite MHA hazard was similar between cohorts (aHR 0.95; 95% CI 0.89-1.02). OHCA survivors had lower hazards for outpatient anxiety/mood (aHR 0.91), psychotic (0.74), and behavioural disorders (0.62); any inpatient psychiatric admission (0.85); inpatient mood disorders (0.69); and deliberate self-harm (0.73). The strongest predictor of new MHA outcomes was pre-existing psychiatric diagnosis (aHR 2.22; 95% CI 1.97-2.49); high pre-arrest ED use, younger age, female sex, and residence in racially marginalized or high-density neighbourhoods also independently predicted risk. Conclusions: Contrary to our hypothesis, OHCA survivors did not exhibit excess MHA risk versus matched critical illness survivors and showed lower hazards across several subcategories, suggesting shared post-ICU rather than arrest-specific psychiatric mechanisms. Nevertheless, nearly half developed a new MHA diagnosis, concentrated in the first six months and driven chiefly by pre-existing psychiatric history. These findings support integrating OHCA survivors into unified post-ICU mental health pathways, with early screening and targeted outreach for those with prior psychiatric diagnoses, high ED use, or residence in disadvantaged communities.
na3a0909f679c: Background: Survival following pediatric out-of-hospital cardiac arrest (OHCA) has improved, yet there is a paucity of research about the long-term outcomes and experiences of survivors and their families. Understanding their experiences will help shape survivor- and co-survivor-centered interventions and outcomes that focus on long-term recovery and well-being. Research Question: What is the lived experience of adolescent/young adult survivors (AYA) of OHCA and their parent co-survivors in survivorship? Aims: This study primarily sought to: (1) gain a deeper understanding of AYA survivors’ and their parents’/legal guardians’ perceptions of life after a CA in survivorship and (2) understand how survivors’ and co-survivors’ needs have changed over time since arrest. Methods: The study was conducted at a large pediatric healthcare system in Southern California using a qualitative phenomenological design. Participants were recruited using purposive, snowball, and convenience sampling. Eligible AYA were aged 10 to 24 years, English-speaking, experienced OHCA between ages 10-18, survived greater than 6 months post-arrest, and were able to verbally articulate their experiences. Parents/legal guardians of eligible AYA were also invited to participate. Each participant completed two semi-structured interviews between October 2025 and March 2026, which were audio-recorded and transcribed. Data were analyzed using inductive thematic analysis informed by the hermeneutic circle. Coding was performed independently by two researchers, resolving discrepancies through consensus. Recruitment continued until thematic saturation was achieved. Results: Nine participants, including both survivors (n=3, 33.3%) and co-survivors (n=6, 66.6%), participated. Survivors were aged 18 to 24 years, and co-survivors were aged 40 to 59 years. Four (44.4%) self-identified as Hispanic or Latino. Five (55.5%) identified as White, two (22.2%) as Asian, and two (22.2%) as Native Hawaiian or Pacific Islander. Among participants, four (44.4%) preferred “she” as their gender pronoun, three (33.3%) preferred “he,” and two (22.2%) preferred not to state. Five overarching themes about survivorship were identified: survivorship (a) is a new normal, (b) means being there, (c) is a physical embodiment, (d) means letting go, and (e) is what meaning we want to give it. Survivors emphasized challenges with self-concept and social reintegration, which is critical in their development stage. Parents described persistent anxiety, adjustment challenges, and advocacy burdens. Both groups highlighted discordance between acute care received and long-term support. Conclusions: AYA survivors of OHCA and their parents experience enduring psychosocial and functional impacts. Findings underscore the need for structured, family-centered, and individualized support throughout survivorship.
n4c664cca3d93: Background: Out-of-hospital cardiac arrest (OHCA) remains a major public health challenge, with persistent variation in outcomes across demographic and clinical subgroups. Evaluating recent trends in hospitalization and survival may identify disparities and inform targeted improvements in resuscitation systems of care. Methods: We conducted a retrospective trend analysis using the Cardiac Arrest Registry to Enhance Survival (CARES) from 2019-2024. We evaluated temporal changes in (1) proportions of hospitalized OHCA patients across demographic and clinical characteristics and (2) survival to hospital discharge stratified by hospitalization-related factors.Generalized linear models with a Poisson distribution and log link were applied separately for each subgroup, with calendar year modeled as a continuous predictor and population at risk included as an offset. Deviance-based corrections accounted for overdispersion. Annual percentage changes with 95% confidence intervals (CIs) were estimated, with p<0.05 indicating statistical significance. Results: Significant shifts in OHCA hospitalization patterns were observed. The proportion of hospitalized female patients declined by 0.60% per year (95% CI, –0.76% to –0.45%; p<0.0001), while male hospitalizations increased by 0.37% per year (95% CI, 0.28% to 0.46%; p<0.0001). Hospitalizations among Black patients decreased modestly (–1.30% per year; 95% CI, –2.56% to –0.03%; p=0.045), whereas Hispanic/Latino patients demonstrated a substantial increase (4.94% per year; 95% CI, 2.17% to 7.79%; p=0.0004).Clinically, the proportion of patients achieving sustained return of spontaneous circulation declined (–2.58% per year; 95% CI, –4.41% to –0.72%; p=0.0066), while hospitalizations without sustained ROSC increased modestly. The proportion pronounced dead in the emergency department decreased significantly (–6.26% per year; 95% CI, –10.24% to –2.10%; p=0.0035).Despite these shifts, no subgroup demonstrated a statistically significant improvement in survival to discharge. Overall survival increased by 1.54% per year (95% CI, –2.18% to 5.39%; p=0.42), with similarly non-significant findings across arrest characteristics and hospitalization factors. Conclusions: From 2019 to 2024, OHCA hospitalization patterns shifted across demographic and clinical subgroups, with persistent disparities and declining sustained ROSC. Despite these changes, survival to hospital discharge has not significantly improved. These findings highlight ongoing inequities and underscore the need for targeted, system-level interventions to improve OHCA outcomes.
n0c968906ca0e: Introduction: Survivorship after cardiac arrest includes cognitive, emotional, and physical aspects of recovery. Domain specific recovery trajectories are individualized and under-reported in the literature. Understanding recovery capacity is critical for optimizing goal setting when counseling patients and their caregivers. Methods: We performed a retrospective analysis of comatose cardiac arrest survivors enrolled in our single-center acute brain injury repository between 2/5/2022 and 12/11/2025. We excluded patients who died prior to hospital discharge or who had no follow up modified Rankin Scale score (mRS). Patients were followed prospectively, and mRS was determined using patient and family interviews. Patients discharged alive with at least one follow-up mRS at any of the four time-points (3-month, 6-month, one year, two years) were included in the analysis. Good outcome was defined as mRS 0-3; longitudinal mRS changes were assessed with a Sankey plot. Results: Among the 56 patients [mean (SD) age 57.7 (16.8) years] included, 89.3% (n=50) were out-of-hospital cardiac arrest. The most common arrest etiology was cardiac (n = 36, 64.3%), of which the majority (n = 26, 72.2%) had a shockable rhythm, followed by respiratory (n = 15, 26.8%). Median (IQR) length of stay was 14 (9-22) days. The most common discharge locations were home (n=31, 55.4%) and short-term rehabilitation (n=14, 25%). Median (IQR) number of mRS assessments was 2 (2-3). Good outcome increased from 23 patients at three months to 26 patients at one year. There was one patient with poor outcome at one-year (mRS 4) who improved to good outcome at two years (mRS 0). In a sub-analysis of patients with an mRS at both 3-months and 1-year (n=11), 4 (36.4%) patients with mRS 2-3 improved to mRS 0-1. Conclusion: Functional neurologic recovery following cardiac arrest varies over time. Understanding recovery trajectories and factors associated with improvement are critical to maximizing survivorship potential. Our preliminary findings convey that recovery can be delayed, and possible up to two years following arrest.
ne85d4bae12e7: Introduction: Even among cardiac arrest survivors discharged with favorable neurologic outcomes, the risk of subsequent cardiac and non-cardiac complications, hospital re-admission, and mortality remains substantial. A better understanding of the causes and predictors of post-discharge re-admission and death is essential to developing targeted follow-up strategies, optimizing long-term recovery, and improving cardiac arrest survivorship. Methods: We performed a retrospective analysis of cardiac arrest survivors enrolled in a single center cardiac arrest recovery program (CARP) between 1/19/2024 and 5/9/2026. The CARP program follows all in-hospital (IHCA) and out-of-hospital cardiac arrest (OHCA) patients from index hospitalization admission to discharge, at which point those who awaken and were following basic commands were enrolled. Enrollment included an evaluation for psychological and cognitive symptoms, as well as post-discharge neurology clinic appointment (on average three months post-discharge). Amongst enrolled patients, hospital re-admissions and mortality occurring prior to post-discharge neurology clinic visit were tracked. Results: Of 105 enrolled patients, 34 (32.4%) underwent hospital readmission. The median [interquartile range] time from index cardiac arrest discharge to re-admission was 16 [8-99.8] days. Eight (7.6% of all patients, 24% of re-admitted patients) died at a median of 71.5 [20-160] days from index hospital discharge. The most common cause of death was withdrawal of life sustaining therapy (50%, n=4), followed by recurrent arrest without ROSC (25%, n=2). Amongst those who survived the readmission, the median [IQR] length of stay was 4 [2-10] days and the most common admission diagnoses included cardiopulmonary dysfunction (n=13, 38.2%) and neuropsychiatric symptoms (n=11, 32.4%). Patients requiring readmission were more likely to have suffered an IHCA, were younger, had longer length of stay, and were less likely to be discharged home (Table 1). Conclusion: Cardiac arrest survivors experience a heightened risk for readmission and mortality, even after discharge with good neurologic outcome. The most common causes for readmission were cardiopulmonary and neurologic symptoms. Further work to help identify those at highest risk for readmission and to evaluate the impact of a nurse navigator on readmission rate and mortality should be prioritized.

nebedc3941d41: A woman aged 35 years was evaluated for a 1-year history of recurrent, brief (approximately 15 min) episodes of non-positional vertigo described as a spinning sensation. n1161c7e208da: Cancer is now one of the defining health and development challenges of our time. The 56 nations of the Commonwealth, home to 2·7 billion people, mirror this global burden. n36711ffe3a9c: One critical shortcoming of many clinical therapeutic trials is their focus on short-term effects, leaving unanswered questions about how participants fare in the longer term. Trial extension studies are conducted to address this gap, allowing assessment of both durability of treatment benefit (eg, whether disease remission or improvements in function are maintained or diminished over time) and long-term safety (such as incidence of delayed adverse events). ne9e8bae073bb: Cancer is a growing health and economic burden worldwide, yet comprehensive global estimates of cancer treatment costs are sparse. We then estimated global and regional treatment costs (overall and by cancer type) in US$ 2022 based on the latest available incidence data from GLOBOCAN. North America and Europe accounted for 64% of total costs, but only 36% of diagnosed cancer cases. Mean costs per diagnosed patient were $38 650 (95% UI 36 070-41 280) globally, ranging from $3380 (95% UI 2960-3820) in eastern Africa to $93 600 (95% UI 87 170-100 150) in North America. n05506f50f3c4: The world has never been wealthier. Yet in 2025, an estimated 831 million people lived on less than US$3 per day. n54c459ca5155: Irritable bowel syndrome, chronic constipation, and functional diarrhoea are disorders of gut–brain interaction, the symptoms of which include abnormal stool consistency or frequency accompanied by varying degrees of abdominal pain, discomfort, bloating, or distension. These conditions affect 20% of the global population with a relapsing and remitting course. Risk factors include female sex, younger age, a history of common mental disorders, and acute enteric infection. The pathophysiology of irritable bowel syndrome, chronic constipation, and functional diarrhoea remain incompletely understood, but are thought to be secondary to aberrant interactions throughout the gut–brain axis, resulting in disordered gut motility and visceral hypersensitivity.
n84da0a1b28c6: Poverty alleviation is a pressing global challenge that is intricately linked with health, as emphasised by the Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs). In 2020, 724 million people were living in extreme poverty, defined as living on less than US$2·15 per person per day at 2017 purchasing power parity, 90 million more than the pre-COVID-19 pandemic UN projection.
n6e0fa2420828: The rapid worldwide spread of antimicrobial resistance among gram-negative bacteria is driven by a complex interplay of human, environmental, and health care-associated factors and accelerated by mobile genetic elements that facilitate the dissemination of resistance genes. Resistance in gram-negative bacteria arises primarily through reduced drug entry, active drug efflux, modification of antibiotic targets, and enzymatic drug inactivation, most notably through β-lactamase production. Clinically important resistant pathogens include extended-spectrum β-lactamase-producing Enterobacterales, carbapenem-resistant Enterobacterales, Pseudomonas aeruginosa with difficult-to-treat resistance, and carbapenem-resistant Acinetobacter baumannii. Limited access to effective antibiotics and the continued emergence of resistance to available agents pose substantial challenges to the management of these infections. Appropriate management requires timely and accurate diagnostics, targeted use of newer β-lactam agents, effective source control, and judicious selection of treatment durations.

nc0f16d18b824: BackgroundVEGFR tyrosine kinase inhibitors (TKIs) are considered the backbone for the treatment of metastatic clear-cell renal cell carcinoma. We hypothesise that the administration of bevacizumab during scheduled breaks in pazopanib (TKI) treatment can improve tolerability and prolong progression-free survival compared with historical controls.MethodsIn this single-arm, phase 1/2 trial in five US academic cancer centres, patients (aged ≥18 years) with histologically confirmed metastatic clear-cell renal cell carcinoma, Eastern Cooperative Oncology Group performance status of 1 or less, and adequate organ functions were included. The phase 1 portion included patients with up to one previous therapy with high-dose IL-2 or an anti-PD-1 compound alone or in combination with a CTLA-4 inhibitor. The phase 2 portion enrolled only patients with treatment-naive metastatic clear-cell renal cell carcinoma. The primary endpoint of phase 1 was to find the recommended phase 2 dose (RP2D). We tested a novel regimen using four dose levels: oral pazopanib (600 or 800 mg daily on days 1-28, followed by a 7 day break) alternating with intravenous bevacizumab (5, 7·5, or 10 mg/kg, one on day 36 and one on day 50) on a 10-week cycle in patients with metastatic clear-cell renal cell carcinoma naive to TKI treatment. The primary endpoint of phase 2 was median progression-free survival, assessed by a masked central statistician review. Dose selection (in patients who had completed 15 weeks) and activity (in patients who had completed one full 10-week cycle of the novel regimen) were analysed in the per-protocol population. Safety analyses included all patients who received any treatment. This trial was registered with ClinicalTrials.gov (NCT01684397) and is ongoing but closed to new participants.FindingsBetween Nov 21, 2012, and June 11, 2018, phase 1 enrolled 25 patients, with 18 patients evaluable for dose-limiting toxicity during the extended 15-week safety assessment period. The RP2D was established as pazopanib 800 mg daily (days 1-28) and bevacizumab 10 mg/kg on days 36 and 50 of a 10-week cycle. Between Jan 23, 2019, and Oct 19, 2023, phase 2 enrolled 53 patients, of whom 51 (including six from phase 1) were evaluable for activity and 59 were evaluable for safety. 36 (71%) patients were male and 15 (29%) were female, and 48 (94%) patients were White. 33 (65%) patients in phase 2 had favourable risk per the International Metastatic Renal Cell Carcinoma Database Consortium categories. After a median follow-up of 63·7 months (IQR 16·2-73·5), median progression-free survival was 24·8 months (95% CI 17·2-34·3). The most common grade 3-4 treatment-related adverse events were hypertension (20 [34%] of 59) and elevated aspartate aminotransferase (seven [12%]) and alanine aminotransferase (ten [17%]). Five (8%) patients discontinued the study for drug-related serious adverse events. No treatment-related deaths occurred.InterpretationThe phase 1 portion identified the safe RP2D. The phase 2 portion showed that this novel regimen has promising antitumour activity in patients with metastatic clear-cell renal cell carcinoma in the predominantly favourable risk group who are naive to treatment. Phase 3 randomised controlled trial data are needed to confirm these findings.FundingThe Roswell Park Comprehensive Cancer Center (RPCCC), US National Cancer Institute (NCI), Novartis.
n6506b49225d2: The TALAPRO-2 trial showed improved radiographic progression-free survival and overall survival with first-line talazoparib plus enzalutamide versus placebo plus enzalutamide in patients with metastatic androgen pathway modulator-resistant prostate cancer (APMR; also referred to as castration-resistant prostate cancer) unselected for homologous recombination repair (HRR) gene alterations treated. In this exploratory analysis, HRR gene alteration status agreement was evaluated in the unselected intention-to-treat cohort between solid tumour tissue prospectively tested using a clinical trial assay based on FoundationOne CDx and retrospectively tested ctDNA samples, collected at screening and assessed using an assay based on FoundationOne Liquid CDx. Tumour burden was categorised as positive or negative (ctDNA tumour fraction detectable or not detectable). Reductions in CTCs, enumerated using CELLSEARCH, were defined as conversion (from five or more cells per 7·5 mL of blood to four or fewer cells per 7·5 mL of blood) or CTC0 (from one or more cells per 7·5 mL of blood to zero). Between Jan 7, 2019, and Sept 17, 2020, 805 patients were enrolled and randomly assigned (402 to talazoparib plus enzalutamide; 403 to placebo plus enzalutamide); median follow-up for radiographic progression-free survival was 24·9 months (IQR 21·9-30·2) for the talazoparib group and 24·6 months (14·4-30·2) for the placebo group. n5fdc6655acc1: BackgroundAmbient artificial intelligence (AI) medical scribes may reduce documentation burden and clinician burnout. Whether use intensity drives benefits remains uncertain.ObjectiveTo evaluate the association between AI scribe (Heidi) enrollment and documentation burden and whether changes differ by use intensity.DesignRetrospective quality improvement study using an interrupted time series (ITS) indexed on each clinician's enrollment month adjusted for patient demographics and visit complexity. A secondary 3-group ITS compared enrolled nonusers, low users, and high users.Setting14-hospital health system in Boston, Massachusetts.Participants902 outpatient clinicians enrolled in Heidi; 605 users and 297 enrolled nonusers.InterventionHeidi enrollment after system-wide implementation beginning January 2025.MeasurementsThe primary outcome was note-active time. Secondary outcomes included same-day and after-hours note closures, note length, and work relative value units (wRVUs).Results1 637 227 encounters had notes authored by enrolled clinicians between 1 July 2024 and 31 January 2026. Enrollment was associated with an immediate reduction in note-active time (-1.21 minutes [95% CI, -1.74 to -0.68 minutes]), with larger reductions among high users (-2.50 minutes [CI, -3.55 to -1.45 minutes]) than nonusers (difference, -2.20 minutes [CI, -3.46 to -0.95 minutes]) and low users (difference, -1.72 minutes [CI, -3.03 to -0.40 minutes]). High users had greater increases in note length than nonusers (difference, +170.90 characters [CI, 21.07 to 320.70 characters]) and low users (difference, +270.70 characters [CI, 131.04 to 410.36 characters]). No differences were observed in same-day closure, after-hours closure, or wRVUs.LimitationObservational design with potential unmeasured confounding; inability to distinguish AI-scribed from clinician-authored notes postenrollment.ConclusionHeidi enrollment was associated with reductions in documentation time and increases in note length, concentrated among high users. Enrollment was not associated with improvements in same-day, after-hours note closures, or wRVUs.Primary funding sourceNone.
n939d3be5d6f9: BackgroundRandomized clinical trials (RCTs) have compared laparoscopic liver resection (LLR) and open liver resection (OLR) for colorectal liver metastases (CRLM); however, long-term outcomes and subgroup effects have not been comprehensively evaluated.PurposeTo compare postoperative and long-term oncologic outcomes after LLR versus OLR for CRLM using individual participant data from RCTs.Data sourcesPubMed, Embase, and Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials were searched from database inception through March 2025 for RCTs comparing LLR and OLR for CRLM.Study selectionEligible studies were RCTs comparing LLR and OLR for CRLM.Data extractionIndividual participant data, including unpublished data, were obtained from trial investigators of all 4 published RCTs.Data synthesisAnalyses used a modified intention-to-treat approach and 1-stage individual participant data meta-analysis (IPDMA) with trial-adjusted regression models and g-computation to estimate standardized treatment effects across outcomes, with 95% CIs obtained by nonparametric bootstrap resampling. Prespecified subgroup analyses assessed heterogeneity of treatment effect for the primary outcome. A total of 761 patients were included (laparoscopic, n = 384; open, n = 377). Postoperative morbidity was lower in patients assigned to laparoscopic surgery compared with open surgery (19% vs. 27%). Among patients who received preoperative systemic therapy, morbidity did not differ between groups (25% vs. 24%). Ninety-day mortality was 1.8% after LLR and 0.8% after OLR. After a median follow-up of 93 months, overall survival and disease-free survival did not differ between groups.LimitationAnalyses were limited to variables available across all studies.ConclusionIn this IPDMA of all published RCTs in the field, LLR for CRLM was associated with lower postoperative morbidity than OLR, with similar long-term oncologic outcomes.Primary funding sourceNone. (PROSPERO: CRD42024502655).
nf1278a57d48b: BackgroundObesity and early-onset cancer are both increasing among young adults, yet evidence remains limited.ObjectiveTo assess associations between obesity and early-onset cancer risk in young adults.DesignNationwide population-based cohort study.SettingKorean National Health Insurance Service database, 2009 to 2021.Patients6 313 338 adults aged 20 to 39 years without prior cancer, from a national health screening program.MeasurementsBody mass index (BMI) was categorized into 5 groups (underweight to class II obesity) according to Asian-specific criteria. The outcome was incident cancer.ResultsDuring a mean follow-up of 11.2 years, 151 893 cancer cases occurred. Ten-year cumulative incidence ranged from 1.84% (95% CI, 1.83% to 1.86%) in the normal-weight group to 2.24% (CI, 2.22% to 2.27%) in class I obesity and 2.62% (CI, 2.56% to 2.68%) in class II obesity, with absolute risk differences of 0.40% (CI, 0.39% to 0.41%) and 0.78% (CI, 0.73% to 0.82%). The relative association was more pronounced in men, and absolute risk differences were greater in women. In combined BMI-waist circumference analyses, people with class I obesity based on BMI and with abdominal obesity had higher 10-year cumulative incidence (2.45% [CI, 2.41% to 2.50%]) than those without abdominal obesity (2.13% [CI, 2.10% to 2.16%]), exceeding that of those with class II obesity without abdominal obesity (2.20% [CI, 2.03% to 2.36%]). The highest cumulative incidence was observed for thyroid, endometrial, and ovarian cancer. Obesity was not associated with higher risk for breast cancer diagnosed by age 50 years.LimitationsObservational design; nonrepresentative sample limited to screening participants; and unmeasured confounding, including smoking burden.ConclusionObesity in young Korean adults, measured by BMI and waist circumference, is associated with higher early-onset cancer risk persisting into midlife, with patterns varying by cancer type. Early weight management may be important for prevention.Primary funding sourceNone.
n0a8e551601ba: Although international guidelines recommend intrauterine insemination (IUI) with ovarian stimulation as first-line treatment for unexplained infertility, evidence from comparisons of this method with in vitro fertilization (IVF) is limited. We conducted a sequential, multicenter, randomized, controlled trial involving couples with unexplained infertility. Stage 1 was a noninferiority comparison between IUI with ovarian stimulation (up to four cycles) and IVF (one complete cycle, with transfer of all embryos). After 7 months, couples without live birth or ongoing pregnancy could proceed to stage 2: couples in the IUI group could undergo up to two IVF cycles, and those in the IVF group could undergo one further IVF cycle. The primary outcome was the cumulative live-birth rate resulting from stage 1. Couples who were in stage 1 during lockdowns due to coronavirus disease 2019 were omitted from the analysis of the primary outcome. A secondary outcome was the cumulative live-birth rate resulting from stages 1 and 2. Live births were included in analyses if day 1 of the treatment cycle that led to pregnancy or day 1 of the last menstrual period before conception occurred within 7 months (stage 1) or 20 months (stage 2) after randomization. The noninferiority margin for the primary outcome was a between-group difference of 10 percentage points. A total of 737 couples underwent randomization: 365 couples were assigned to undergo IUI with ovarian stimulation before IVF, and 372 were assigned to undergo first-line IVF (1 couple in the IVF group withdrew consent for the use of data). The primary-outcome analysis included 585 couples (288 in the IUI group and 297 in the IVF group). The cumulative live-birth rate from stage 1 was 31% (89 births among 288 couples) with IUI with ovarian stimulation and 55% (164 births among 297 couples) with IVF (adjusted risk difference, -24 percentage points; 95% confidence interval [CI], -31 to -16). The cumulative live-birth rate from stages 1 and 2 among all the couples who had undergone randomization and provided consent was 70% (257 births among 365 couples) and 71% (265 births among 371 couples), respectively (adjusted risk difference, 0 percentage points; 99% CI, -9 to 8). Overall, serious adverse events occurred in 6 couples in the IUI group and in 14 couples in the IVF group; most serious adverse events were related to oocyte retrieval or hyperstimulation. In couples with unexplained infertility, treatment with four cycles of IUI with ovarian stimulation was not noninferior to treatment with one complete cycle of IVF with respect to the cumulative live-birth rate. n1d78a20a6861: The treatment landscape of EGFR-mutated non-small-cell lung cancer harbouring exon 19 deletion or L858R mutations has advanced remarkably over the past two decades. nbf23cba0be20: BackgroundNational cancer control plans (NCCPs) vary in scope and comprehensiveness, yet expert-led review is resource intensive and limits cross-country comparability. We aimed to assess NCCP comprehensiveness across 50 countries using the policy reasoning integrated sequential model (PRISM), a validated multiagent artificial intelligence (AI) system.MethodsWe identified the most recent national NCCP for each country from the International Cancer Control Partnership repository, the WHO Noncommunicable Disease Document Repository, and government websites; sub-national plans, broader non-communicable disease or health-sector strategies, drafts, and superseded versions were excluded. We developed an analytical framework of 12 elements and 76 sub-elements, aligned with WHO, International Cancer Control Partnership, and Union for International Cancer Control guidance and validated it through a modified two-stage Delphi process (online survey of 67 experts; triangulation workshop with 31 participants). PRISM comprised document ingestion (Qwen2.5-VL-72B), policy analysis with retrieval-augmented generation (Llama 4 Scout, 109B), and semantic quality assurance. PRISM was validated against masked dual-expert ratings for six purposely selected NCCPs, then applied to all NCCPs. Scores were normalised to 0-5 and medians compared across World Bank income group and WHO region.FindingsWe identified 50 NCCPs that met the inclusion criteria. Median overall comprehensiveness was 2·78 (IQR 2·25-3·09), with high comprehensiveness classified as 4·0-5·0, moderate as 2·0-3·9, and low as 0-1·9. Europe (2·96; 2·78-3·35) and lower-middle-income countries (2·97; 2·48-3·15) had the highest medians; the western Pacific (2·21; 1·78-2·87) and low-income countries (2·05; 1·94-2·22) had the lowest. Element-level medians were highest for implementation (4·17; 3·54-4·38), health services (3·89; 2·63-4·19), and governance and organisation (3·67; 3·35-3·98), and lowest for financing (1·88; 1·00-2·69), outcomes (1·83; 1·33-2·33), and threats (2·19; 1·72-2·34). Financing showed the largest gaps-only five of eleven financing sub-elements had median scores of 1·0 or less.InterpretationOur analysis suggests that NCCP comprehensiveness varies substantially between countries with consistent weaknesses in financing, outcome measurement, and contextual analysis. A shared health systems framework and scalable AI appraisal tools, such as PRISM, could support more complete, comparable, and actionable plans to strengthen cancer control globally by providing the possibility for rapid analysis of comprehensiveness of NCCPs and generation of timely, achievable, and evidence-informed, context-specific plans that use the latest data.FundingHarvard University.
neb745a437649: Patients with de novo metastatic nasopharyngeal carcinoma were historically deemed incurable and treated with palliative intent. Emergence of potent systemic therapy in combination with local treatment for both locoregional and metastatic diseases has enabled long-term survival in some patients. This international guideline was developed through consensus-building by 54 experts from 46 centres across 18 countries or regions and endorsed by 17 oncology organisations. 32 recommendations across seven clinical domains were formulated, including 29 strong (≥80% agreement [consensus] or high quality of evidence) and three conditional recommendations (67-79% agreement). We recommend that curative-intent treatment should be offered to medically fit patients with no more than three metastatic lesions in two or fewer organs at baseline or following response to systemic therapy; multimodality treatment (comprising immunochemotherapy, locoregional radiotherapy, metastasis-directed therapy, and maintenance therapy) is recommended. This guideline provides a practical framework for standardisation of clinical management of de novo metastatic nasopharyngeal carcinoma and identification of key evidence gaps for future research.
n9b8e8ddc7353: Up to 12% of childhood cancer survivors have an underlying cancer predisposition syndrome (CPS). As a result, these childhood cancer survivors are at increased risk for developing and succumbing to subsequent malignant neoplasms. Identifying childhood cancer survivors with CPS is essential to improving overall outcomes by informing tailored approaches to cancer screening, treatment, and, for some, risk-reducing interventions. Despite these potential benefits, it is often unclear which childhood cancer survivors warrant referral for genetic counselling and germline genetic testing. Using an evidence-based approach, a standardised guideline for referral for cancer genetics evaluation of childhood cancer survivors at high risk of having a CPS was developed and incorporated into the Children's Oncology Group Long-Term Follow-Up Guidelines for Survivors of Childhood, Adolescent, and Young Adult Cancers. This Policy Review details the importance, development, and anticipated impact of this new guideline. Raising awareness of this guideline is crucial to enhancing the integration of genetics into survivorship care and improving health outcomes for childhood cancer survivors with CPS.
n499627ac072d: BackgroundAnti-CD19 CAR T-cell therapy is the standard second-line treatment for patients with relapsed or refractory large B-cell lymphoma. However, there is no evidence from randomised controlled trials in patients ineligible for transplantation. To address this gap, we compared zamtocabtagene autoleucel (zamto-cel), a CAR T-cell therapy directed at CD20 and CD19, with rituximab-gemcitabine-oxaliplatin (R-GemOx) chemoimmunotherapy in patients ineligible for transplantation with relapsed or refractory large B-cell lymphoma.MethodsDALY 2-EU is an open-label, multicentre, randomised, phase 2 trial conducted at 45 centres across 12 countries in Europe. naabad6018a64: Offering late-line systemic therapy to patients with chemo-refractory metastatic colorectal cancer demands a careful estimation of the balance between the expected treatment benefit and its potential impact on quality of life, including adverse events, hospital visits, and psychosocial consequences.1 In such a comprehensive and individualised assessment of patients’ general conditions, usually summarised by Eastern Cooperative Oncology Group (ECOG) performance status, the cumulative burden of disease-related symptoms and previous treatment-related adverse events, together with the potential decay of organ functional reserve, cannot be neglected.
n37e38146b6c7: Remibrutinib was superior to teriflunomide in patients with relapsing multiple sclerosis, while maintaining a favourable safety profile. These findings support remibrutinib as a potential new oral treatment option for relapsing multiple sclerosis.
neade2a36331e: Large-scale genome-wide association studies have identified hundreds of multiple sclerosis risk loci, most of which implicate immune pathways and establish multiple sclerosis as a highly polygenic, immune-mediated disease. n4151c8f48c2e: BackgroundPancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC) has poor outcomes and high rates of locoregional recurrence. n2f70a03ce0f8: Heavy menstrual bleeding is a challenging condition that, when refractory to conventional treatment, frequently culminates in hysterectomy. n7782c90086eb: For decades, the standard of care for patients with resected stage II and III colon cancer has centred on surgery with consideration of postoperative adjuvant systemic therapy to reduce risk of recurrence. nf56aff0ef588: BackgroundMedicare Advantage insurers conduct in-home health risk assessments (HRAs) to identify high-risk patients and facilitate appropriate care. n98f014590d8e: BackgroundThe Choosing Wisely initiative made recommendations where screening, testing, or treatment may be overused, with caveats around appropriate use. n1b491eba192b: The Hindu Kush Himalayan region, also known as the Third Pole, is warming faster than the global average, with mountain environments experiencing particularly rapid climatic change and climatic extremes.1 The potential risks of glacial lake outburst floods (GLOFs) have been documented for decades, with 47 glacial lakes at risk of expansion and causing GLOFs located in the Hindu Kush Himalayan region, including 21 in Nepal.2 The Rasuwa-Bhote Koshi flood of Aug 26, 2026, near the China–Nepal border, resulted in a catastrophic flood travelling at a speed of 188 km/h from its source; the flood covered 20 km within 7–8 min and reached the China–Nepal border at Rasuwagadhi.

n388921f77d7b: The Victorian painter Richard Dadd was born in 1817. By the time of his death in 1886 he had been detained in psychiatric hospitals for 42 years. nc323dcc0f863: The discovery of antibody-mediated glial and neuronal disorders has transformed the diagnosis and treatment of neurological diseases previously considered idiopathic or not recognised as immune-mediated. Antibody-mediated disorders targeting glial aquaporin-4 and myelin oligodendrocyte glycoprotein are distinct nosological entities, defined by specific targets, mechanisms, syndromes, and therapeutic implications. By contrast, antibody-mediated disorders targeting neuronal antigens (ie, autoimmune encephalitides) are still frequently analysed collectively, with data from different disorders pooled as if they represent a single disease rather than distinct entities. Evidence from anti-NMDA receptor encephalitis, anti-LGI1 encephalitis, and anti-IgLON5 disease (used here as exemplars of autoimmune encephalitides) indicates that individual autoimmune encephalitides differ in demographics, triggers, mechanisms, clinical manifestations, post-acute trajectories, and treatment requirements. The broad, heterogeneous presentations of autoimmune encephalitides require coordinated multidisciplinary care within and beyond neurology, involving specialists in paediatrics, infectious diseases, epilepsy, movement disorders, sleep medicine, intensive care, cognitive rehabilitation, and other relevant disciplines. Such interdisciplinary collaboration facilitates the recognition of new diseases and elucidation of the causes of previously unclassified disorders. Improving patient care requires not only aetiological and mechanistic insight to enable development of targeted therapies but also strengthened cross-specialty expertise to optimise diagnosis and management.
n5729197f38e9: Traumatic brain injury (TBI) and spinal cord injury (SCI) affect more than 220 million people worldwide and are associated with cardiometabolic, endocrine, neurological, and psychiatric sequelae for years to decades after an acute injury. However, most health systems still treat neurotrauma (TBI and SCI, collectively) as a time-limited event, leaving long-term surveillance of these patients fragmented or absent, which leads to preventable mortality and avoidable readmissions. TBI and SCI in adults should be reclassified as acute-onset multisystem chronic-risk conditions. Existing cardiovascular, endocrine, and psychiatric services do not capture neurotrauma-specific risks, including trauma-induced hypopituitarism, autonomic dysregulation, accelerated ageing, and cognitive-behavioural impairment, so neurotrauma care is best framed as a missing node in chronic neurological care. n610f679f14c5: Health professionals and policy makers should fully support the students currently protesting in France.1 Apart from the regrettable outbursts of violence happening during protests, this movement reflects the anger of youth at decades of successive policies, both at national and global levels, which have progressively widened educational inequalities. These educational inequalities have led to a cascade of further inequalities: access to employment and type of employment (manual or office-based); level of income—in the past 20 years, the Gini index in France increased from 0·27 to 0·30;2 living conditions and the environment (quality of food, water, noise, air, etc); and, eventually, health inequities.
n1d8ac6a16ca9: Degenerative cervical myelopathy (DCM), the most common non-traumatic spinal cord injury, is a prevalent, progressive, and highly disabling neurological disease, causing heterogeneous impairment ranging from sensory loss and impaired hand dexterity to gait, balance, and autonomic dysfunction. Disability often persists despite surgical decompression, and untreated disease can progress to irreversible neurological injury, including tetraplegia. Current clinical management is largely reactive, with diagnosis and intervention typically only after neurological deterioration has become clinically apparent and radiographic evidence of cervical myelopathy is established. Advances in multimodal diagnostics over the past 5 years are now enabling the detection of subtle spinal cord injury, biological disease activity, and subclinical neurodegeneration before overt clinical disability. Quantitative spinal cord MRI, advanced neurophysiological assessments, dynamic biomechanical metrics, and sensitive functional testing provide complementary tools for early detection, risk stratification, and prognostication. Together, these approaches are redefining DCM as a disease that should be managed proactively. Evidence supports decompressive surgery in patients with moderate-to-severe disease, whereas in milder disease or in spinal stenosis that might develop into DCM, the management of patients should be interdisciplinary, with active surveillance to detect early deterioration or decompressive surgery in selected cases. Improved prediction of disease trajectories and clearer evidence on long-term outcomes could enable selective earlier intervention and help to prevent neurological disability.
